projects.title: Guest Pass

card.summary: Designed temporary door access for LenelS2's Elements platform. Hosts create a pass, guests unlock from their phone, and credentials expire automatically. Shipped Q4 2021.

sections.title: Guest Pass
sections.summary: Temporary door access for LenelS2's Elements platform. Hosts create a pass, share a link, and guests unlock doors from their phone before credentials expire automatically.

blocks.heading: The challenge
blocks.body: Before Guest Pass, granting visitor access in Elements required creating a full person record, normally reserved for employees, and manually revoking it later. Customers needed a way to grant temporary visitors access without creating permanent credentials or coordinating access through the lobby.

blocks.heading: The solution
blocks.body: Hosts create a pass by setting start and end times, assigning door readers, and sharing a link. Guests open the pass on their phone and tap to unlock. When the access window closes, the pass is deleted automatically with no lingering credentials.

blocks.heading: Context
blocks.body: LenelS2 develops physical security software for access control, video, and mobile credentials. Elements is their cloud platform for managing badge readers and cameras across a facility.

aside.body: Released in Q4 2021. The feature is included in sales demonstrations and has generated ongoing requests for additional capability.

sections.heading: What the feature had to do
sections.intro: Hosts and guests do different jobs on the same pass, and security teams need an event log when someone actually uses it.

items: Hosts issue and send passes themselves and remain responsible for the guest
A way to share the pass, plus an email template
The ability to update a pass after sending
Guests receive the pass by email with a link to a web UI
The UI shows the validity window and who issued it
One unlock button per assigned reader
The Elements event feed records when a pass is used and at which reader

sections.heading: From a low-fi flow to the shipped UI
sections.intro: Flow first in InVision Freehand, then hi-fi in Figma using the LenelS2 design system I helped maintain.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.1 — InVision Freehand flow: create, share, use, and manage a guest pass.

items.title: 1. Guest pass list
items.body: A dedicated area of Elements where hosts see active, scheduled, and expired passes.

items.title: 2. Create a pass
items.body: Name, activation and expiration, then readers. In hi-fi I replaced the recipient field with a share step.

blocks.heading: Sharing became its own step
blocks.body: In the low-fidelity flow, the recipient email lived inside the create form, which meant any edit risked re-sending the pass. I moved sharing to its own screen so hosts can copy the link through any channel, and edits no longer notify the guest.

sections.heading: Animation as feedback
sections.intro: Guest passes live on standalone pages outside the main Elements interface, which allowed animated unlock buttons that confirm the tap registered at the door.

items.title: Unlock success
items.body: Confirmation animation after a guest taps to unlock a door reader.

items.title: Unlock error
items.body: Feedback when a pass is invalid, expired, or the reader cannot be reached.

blocks.title: Code reference
blocks.body: An HTML and CSS translation of the prototype to give engineering a concrete implementation reference.

sections.heading: Results & outcomes
sections.statement: Guest Pass released in Q4 2021. It is included in sales demonstrations and has generated ongoing requests for additional functionality.

takeaways.title: Two users, one feature
takeaways.body: Designing for a system owner and a one-time visitor required two separate interfaces on a shared data model, with clear ownership of decisions for each audience.

takeaways.title: Flows first in a complex system
takeaways.body: Mapping the end-to-end flow before high-fidelity design surfaced the re-send problem early, when restructuring was still inexpensive.

takeaways.title: Motion earns its keep at the door
takeaways.body: Unlock animation gives guests immediate confirmation at the door and reduces repeated taps on the reader.

projects.problem: Temporary door access for LenelS2's Elements platform. Hosts create a pass, guests unlock from their phone, and credentials expire automatically.

caseStudy.title: Overview
paragraphs: Guest Pass is a feature I designed for Elements, LenelS2's cloud access control platform, during my co-op in 2021.

The host sets when the pass starts and ends, picks which door readers the guest can reach, and shares a link. The guest opens it on their phone and taps unlock. When the window closes, the pass deletes itself.
It released in Q4 2021. The feature is included in sales demonstrations and has generated ongoing requests for additional capability.

caseStudy.title: Who is LenelS2?
paragraphs: LenelS2 develops physical security software for access control, video, and mobile credentials. Elements is their cloud platform for managing badge readers and cameras across a facility.

caseStudy.title: What is Elements?
paragraphs: Elements is LenelS2's SaaS platform for access control and video management. Companies use it to monitor facilities with cameras and badge readers.

caseStudy.title: Problem
paragraphs: Before Guest Pass, granting visitor access in Elements required creating a full person record, normally reserved for employees, and manually revoking it later.
Customers needed a way to grant temporary visitors access without creating permanent credentials or coordinating access through the lobby.

caseStudy.title: Solution
paragraphs: Create a temporary guest pass that activates and deletes itself according to the host's settings.

caseStudy.title: Users
bullets: A person who works at a company and is inviting a guest to their company’s facility (e.g., a hiring manager inviting someone for an interview, or management inviting a business client for a meeting)
A guest who was invited to the company’s facility

subsections.title: Issuing a Guest Pass
bullets: Users need to be able to add guest passes and send them themselves as they are responsible for the guest
Optional start/end date
Assign door readers to the guest pass
A method to share the guest pass
An email template for when a guest pass is shared
The ability to update a guest pass

subsections.title: Using a Guest Pass
bullets: Guest can receive their guest pass via email with link to web UI
UI shows when the pass is valid for and the customer (who will be issuing the guest pass)
Buttons available for each reader to unlock

subsections.title: Events
bullets: Events in the Elements event feed shows when a guest pass is used and where it was used

I mapped the flow in InVision Freehand, then moved to hi-fi in Figma using the LenelS2 design system I helped maintain.
bullets: User navigates to the “Guest Passes” area of Elements
User selects the add button to add a guest pass
User inputs a name, activation and expiration dates and times, and the recipient email
User adds readers
User generates the pass
In high fidelity I moved sharing to its own screen so edits do not re-send the pass. Hosts can copy the link through any channel they prefer.

caseStudy.title: Guest-Facing UI & Animation
paragraphs: {{artifact:Guest UI (open animation)}}
{{artifact:Guest UI (error animation)}}
Once creation was designed, I built the guest-facing web UI.
Guest passes live on standalone pages outside the main Elements interface, which allowed animated unlock buttons that confirm the tap registered at the door.
I built an HTML and CSS reference of the unlock animations in CodePen [here](https://codepen.io/JEScarani/pen/oNWKmxG).

caseStudy.title: Conclusion & Results
paragraphs: Guest Pass served two distinct audiences, the organization running Elements and the guest using temporary access.
The project strengthened my ability to map flows in a complex system and use animation to improve perceived responsiveness.
It released in Q4 2021 and is included in sales demonstrations, with ongoing requests for additional functionality.

constraints: Needed to fit within an existing product ecosystem and patterns
Had to support pass issuers and visiting guests as separate user groups
process: Defined users, roles, permissions, and key workflows (issuer + guest)
Mapped end-to-end flow (create pass → share → use → manage/expire)
Created low-fi flow and wireframes (InVision Freehand)
Produced hi-fi designs in Figma using the LenelS2 design system
Designed guest-facing web UI and button animations for clearer feedback
impact: Drove follow-up feature requests from customers

projects.title: JRCS Command Task

heroImage.alt: JRCS Command Task project cover image

card.summary: Time-boxed design challenge for collision warnings on a shipboard command display, balancing visibility with the need to preserve critical navigation information.

sections.title: JRCS Command Task
sections.summary: Design challenge to warn a ship's bridge of an imminent collision without obscuring other critical navigation information.

blocks.heading: The problem
blocks.body: JRCS Digital Innovation Lab develops a command application that gives captains and officers navigation information for their vessel and highlights nearby traffic through AR. The team provided two existing screens and asked me to design a collision warning pattern.

blocks.heading: Users
blocks.body: Captains and watch officers who monitor dense navigation displays for extended periods.

items: Must carry enough information to act on
Cannot drown out any other critical information

sections.heading: Sketches to shipped-looking UI
sections.intro: My first approach was a popover pointing at the vessel on a collision course. After testing three shapes, a rectangular window provided the necessary detail without obscuring the chart.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.1 — The two screens provided at the start of the challenge.

items.title: 1. Sketches
items.body: Three popover shapes and a warning treatment for the compass-like view. I also explored projected ship paths and removed that concept because it would be difficult to implement in rough seas and computationally expensive.

items.title: 2. Lo-fi wireframes
items.body: Narrowing to the primary view and comparing a couple of popover structures.

items.title: 3. Hi-fi progression
items.body: Styled to the application's existing UI standards, then refined with clearer labels and a boat indicator.

items.title: 4. Popover in context
items.body: The warning sitting on the real bridge display, competing with everything else on screen.

blocks.heading: Peripheral attention from game UI patterns
blocks.body: First-person shooters such as Halo and Call of Duty use edge-of-screen cues to signal urgency without blocking the view. I applied that pattern as a pulsing red bar at the top of the display. It reaches peripheral vision without covering navigation data.

sections.heading: Legible at sunrise, sunset, and night
sections.intro: A warning must remain legible across lighting conditions. I evaluated the design against sunrise, sunset, and night backgrounds and tested it with color-blind simulation filters so red was not the only signal.

items.caption: Figure 3.1 — Transparency compared across sunrise, sunset, and night backgrounds.
Figure 3.2 — The warning under color-blind simulation filters.

sections.heading: How it ended
sections.statement: The team responded positively to the work, although the role ultimately went to another candidate. It remains one of the most engaging problems I have worked on.

takeaways.title: Feasibility is a design constraint
takeaways.body: The projected-path concept was the strongest early sketch and the first removed from scope. Rough seas and computational cost determined that decision, not visual preference.

takeaways.title: Borrow from outside the domain
takeaways.body: Game interfaces have long addressed the problem of urgent but non-blocking alerts. That research direction informed the pulsing bar more than a review of competing maritime products.

takeaways.title: Prioritize under a time box
takeaways.body: With limited domain context, framing users and requirements up front was what made the rest of the work defensible.

projects.title: Vendor-Client Gateway Redesign

heroImage.alt: Vendor-Client Gateway Redesign project cover image

card.summary: Led the phase-1 redesign of CobbleStone's vendor-facing portal with responsive layouts, clearer information architecture, and reduced client-side configuration options.

sections.title: Vendor-Client Gateway
sections.summary: External-facing portal for CobbleStone's contract management platform. The experience was outdated, difficult to use, and underperforming with clients.

blocks.heading: The challenge
blocks.body: The Vendor Client Gateway is an add-on for Contract Insights, CobbleStone's procurement and contract platform. Clients and support staff had raised concerns for years about a non-responsive layout, outdated UI patterns, and per-client customization that often reduced usability.

blocks.heading: The solution
blocks.body: During a broader UX initiative across the platform, I led the Gateway redesign with responsive layouts, clearer navigation, UI patterns aligned to Contract Insights, and a narrower set of configuration options.

blocks.heading: Where it sits
blocks.body: This work is phase 1 of a three-phase roadmap to redesign existing features, expand capabilities, and iterate based on live feedback.

aside.body: Increase adoption of a module clients had been avoiding by removing the friction that limited everyday use.

sections.heading: What was going wrong
sections.intro: An audit of the existing gateway and review of comparable vendor portals identified four problems to address first.

items.title: Not responsive
items.body: Vendors working away from a desk encountered a desktop-only layout on mobile devices.

items.title: Dated patterns
items.body: Interactions that no longer matched what users expect anywhere else, which hurt both usability and trust.

items.title: Over-customization
items.body: Clients could configure the interface into states that reduced usability for their vendors.

items.title: Inconsistent workflows
items.body: Solicitation and contract management behaved differently depending on where you entered them.

blocks.title: Home
blocks.note: From a configurable wall of widgets to a clear starting point.

blocks.title: Solicitations
blocks.note: The module's highest-traffic workflow, standardized end to end.

blocks.title: News
blocks.note: Announcements that vendors could actually scan.

sections.heading: Results & outcomes
sections.statement: Phase 1 establishes patterns that make the module easier to adopt. The next two phases will build on that foundation.

takeaways.title: Less configurability can be the feature
takeaways.body: Removing configuration options was the most difficult stakeholder conversation and the most meaningful improvement. Flexibility that allows clients to degrade their vendors' experience is not worth preserving.

takeaways.title: Audit before you redesign
takeaways.body: Documenting what existed and why it had been added made the case for standardization more persuasive than visual inspiration alone.

takeaways.title: A mature product moves in phases
takeaways.body: Sequencing the work as redesign, then expand, then iterate kept scope honest and gave engineering something shippable at each step.
